question: In an ordinary attack, when must the target be declared relative to choosing combat cards? Who chooses and commits a card first, is the attack card face up or face down while the defender decides whether to defend, and when are the cards revealed? May the attacker wait to see the defense card and then choose a different attack card or target?
expected_answer: Declare the target first. The attacker then chooses a permitted attack card from hand and plays it face down. Only then may the defender choose a permitted defense card and place it face down, or decline to defend, without first seeing the attack card. Reveal both chosen cards simultaneously. The ordinary procedure commits the target and attack card before seeing the defense; the attacker cannot wait for the defense reveal to choose a different attack card or target.
required_answer_facts: Declare the attack target before either player chooses and commits their combat card.
The attacker chooses and plays the permitted attack card face down first.
The defender then chooses a permitted defense card face down or declines, without seeing the attack card first.
Both chosen cards are revealed simultaneously after those choices.
The target and attack card are already committed before defense reveal; no selecting a different attack card or retargeting after seeing the defense under the ordinary procedure.

exact_source_support: As the attacker, you must choose an attack card from your hand and play it face down in front of you
Then the defender may (but is not required to) choose a defense card from their hand and place it face down in front of them
Once both players have chosen their cards, reveal them at the same time.
distinct_new_branch: Target declaration and hidden attacker commitment precede defender choice; the attacker cannot make or revise those choices after defense information is revealed.

why_substantive: Reversing the source sequence exposes the attack before the defense decision or lets the attacker select/retarget after knowing the defense. Those choices change legal play and information, not just cosmetic wording/card orientation trivia.
